Building houses, bridges, aircraft, cars, and ships requires knowledge of the strength of concrete, steel, plastics, and other materials.
Knowing stiffness at small deformations is not enough: behavior at larger deformation, during unloading, and at eventual failure also matters.
These properties are mainly obtained through experiments on particular materials, specimens, and loading conditions.

**Ultimate strength and factor of safety**
For the kind of material shown here, unloading beyond the elastic limit may shorten the specimen somewhat but leave extension that cannot be recovered.

To provide a strength margin, this lesson takes the allowable stress $\sigma_{\text{allowable}}$ of a structure below the ultimate strength of its material.
The textbook defines the factor of safety as the ratio of ultimate strength to allowable stress:
$n=\frac{\sigma_{\text{ultimate}}}{\sigma_{\text{allowable}}}$.
